plate.subject: ancient banners over a newly united realm at dawn

paragraphs.text: The First Age lasted 1,675 years. It began with Aen’s victory in the War of Men, when the first kingdom of men, Aenor, was founded in the Middle Lands; that victory is Year 1 of the age, and the centuries of fighting before it are not counted. It ended with the close of the first war against Volgan, after the Battle of Dardan and the failed invasion of the Ember Lands. The age that followed is called the Age of Rebuilding.

Men had lived for many generations long before Aen. They had kingdoms, fought one another and kept their own customs, and great realms of men rose and fell in that deep past, but none of them held one crown over all men. Some of the earliest men were stronger, longer-lived and more open to magic than the men of later ages. There was something godlike in their power, although they were still men and not gods.

sources.section: 1. Before the First Age: the birth of Aen

paragraphs.text: The first half of the age is remembered as prosperous. Farming, trade, roads, shipbuilding and exploration spread beyond the Middle Lands. Aenoran ships reached the West Lands, the North Lands, the East Lands, the Cold Lands and the southern islands. Then came successive bad kings, struggles over the succession, wars and revolts, and the great kingdom slowly weakened.

sources.section: 2. The first half of the First Age: peace and expansion

paragraphs.text: In the second millennium of the age the Great Spirit Volgan invaded Mirolon. His armies took Aenor’s royal city and brought the kingdom to the edge of collapse. King Edran, the greatest king of men after Aen, gathered the Grand Alliance against him and broke him at Dardan, where millions died. Edran’s invasion of the Ember Lands then failed against Elzon, and the armies of the alliance went home. Year 1675 closed the age.

sources.section: 4. The rise of Volgan and the fall of the capital
5. The new king and the Grand Alliance
8. The end of the age and its legacy

paragraphs.text: The age left a long inheritance. Aenor survived, but its capital, its institutions, its people and its friendships abroad were badly damaged. Volgan lived on in exile in the Void. Elzon and the last armies of the Ember Lands survived. Dardan lay waste. The elves trusted Aenor’s kings less than before, and the old quarrel of the West Lands with Aenor over its settlements and claims was not settled.

sources.section: 8. The end of the age and its legacy

paragraphs.text: The chronicles agree on the length of the age and the order of its great events, and on little else in their dates. No chronicle tells the names and reigns of most of the kings who ruled between Aen and Edran, and it is not known in which year of the last years of the age Dardan was fought.

sources.section: 9. Suggested dates within the First Age

plate.subject: hosts of ancient men under many kings' banners

paragraphs.text: Before the First Age the kingdoms of men fought one another for hundreds of years. In that long struggle Aen, the fatherless First Man born of magic and power, defeated or united the rival rulers. The war killed many thousands. It ended in his victory and the founding of Aenor, the first united kingdom of men, in the Middle Lands. That victory is Year 1 of the First Age, and the new unity brought centuries of peace.

The early kingdoms fought over rights of inheritance, over fertile land, and over whether any single crown of men should exist at all. Several kings refused the idea of one crown. Others allied with Aen, submitted to him for protection, or resisted until their own cities lay in ruins. Some opposed him because they saw his claimed destiny as a threat to their peoples, even while they knew his nature was beyond the common measure of men.

Aen joined victories, oaths, negotiated submission and royal law into one realm. Its first law was the Peace of the One Crown. The lords kept their own inheritance and custom, but none might make war on another without the judgement of the crown. Breaking that peace was the first meaning of rebellion in the law of Aenor.

For the people of Aenor, the victory ended the wars of rival kings. For the conquered houses, the same victory was the loss of their freedom, and some kept the memory of occupation alive in their own genealogies and chronicles. Many later dynasties descended from Aen’s many sons, and their rival claims troubled Aenor in the years of its decline.
No chronicle tells how the war began, which battles decided it, which kings stood on each side, how many died in all, or by what means Aen at last prevailed.

Aen was exceptional even in the ancient world. He is called the First Man and First of His Name because he was born of magic and power without a direct father, not because he was the first of human kind. He is held to be the greatest man who ever lived, and his blood is counted the most royal of all the lines of men. He is remembered dark-haired and bearded, crowned, in a cloak of black and red, with a very powerful presence.

sources.section: 1. Before the First Age: the birth of Aen

paragraphs.text: His victory in the War of Men founded Aenor, the first kingdom of men, in the Middle Lands, and began Year 1 of the First Age. It brought centuries of peace to the central realm, even while settlement on its distant frontiers remained violent. Aen himself had fought in that war for hundreds of years.

Aen lived for more than four hundred years and had hundreds of sons, and one of them was Ein. Many noble houses of later ages descend from him, but not every man of the early world was of his blood. The old name Ainu is linked with him and with the First Men, but it is not known whether it means Aen’s own line, all the First Men, or some other ancient people.

sources.section: 1. Before the First Age: the birth of Aen

paragraphs.text: The lords who knelt to Aen kept their local inheritance and their customs, but the crown alone could judge a war between them. So the kingdom held together, while the houses he had conquered kept their own memory of the day they lost their freedom.

No chronicle tells where Aen first appeared or what power caused his birth, nor when he died or who reigned after him. The likeness of the names Aen and Aenor is plain, but no chronicle says that the kingdom was named for him.

plate.subject: ships leaving a harbour for a far western shore

paragraphs.text: Aenor’s victory brought centuries of peace to the central realm, and the first half of the First Age is remembered as prosperous. Farming, trade, roads, shipbuilding and exploration spread beyond the Middle Lands. That prosperity was real inside much of Aenor, but settlement on the frontiers was often violent.

sources.section: 2. The first half of the First Age: peace and expansion

paragraphs.text: Aenoran explorers and settlers reached the West Lands, which already had peoples and kingdoms of their own. Aenoran settlements, trading posts and claims led to repeated wars with them, and that hostility survives in the Fourth Age. A wide sea parts the West Lands from the Middle Lands, so rule over them always depended on ships, ports, local friends and contact that came and went.

sources.section: 2. The first half of the First Age: peace and expansion

paragraphs.text: The kingdom made an alliance with the North Lands. Its traders reached the peoples of the East Lands, sometimes called Easterlings, and roads to more distant peoples. Voyages reached the Cold Lands, the southern islands and other eastern and southern shores. Much of what the charts of Aoaz show today was first found in this period.

sources.section: 2. The first half of the First Age: peace and expansion

paragraphs.text: The Ember Lands were exceptionally hard to reach. Their southern heat and the dangerous seas around them turned back ordinary expeditions, and men could chart distant coasts without knowing the lands beyond them. In the north, Zol’s Mistake was already a desolate and nearly unusable waste. Zol had come there long before Aen, and his power there lay comparatively dormant through the First Age.

sources.section: 2. The first half of the First Age: peace and expansion

paragraphs.text: The Roads of Aen, and the sea charts drawn after them, became a source of royal prestige. The kings of Aenor held that early discovery gave them sovereignty over the far shores. The peoples of the West Lands rejected the claim, for they had lived on those shores long before Aenoran ships arrived. Both histories are still told, and both are still used.

sources.section: 2. The first half of the First Age: peace and expansion

paragraphs.text: No chronicle tells how far Aenor’s early rule in the West Lands truly reached.

After the long prosperous centuries, successive bad kings, struggles over the succession, wars and revolts weakened Aenor. The great distances between the crownlands, the frontier settlements and the allied lands made the kingdom ever harder to govern. Rival descendants of Aen competed for the right to rule. Parts of the West Lands resisted Aenor’s authority, and old enemies used every quarrel inside the kingdom.

Aen’s hundreds of sons left a lasting problem. Many noble lines truly descended from him, so a disputed succession was rarely about whether a claimant carried Aen’s blood. It was about which branch had the lawful right to rule, which oaths still held, and whose account of Aen’s wishes the realm would accept. Later kings used his name to justify deeds he had never approved.

The core of the kingdom stayed strong enough to put down each revolt, but its victories emptied its treasury and spent its veterans. Provincial governors gathered taxes for themselves, the old roads decayed, and distant garrisons began to act on their own. The look of order in the capital hid a kingdom less and less able to meet a great invasion.
No chronicle tells the names, reigns and histories of the kings of Aenor between Aen and Edran.

plate.subject: a royal city burning under a southern storm

paragraphs.text: Volgan is a Great Spirit of extraordinary antiquity. Before he founded his own realm he served a New God, somehow overpowered that god, and made himself an independent dominion in the Ember Lands, south of the Middle Lands. No chronicle tells the name of that New God or how their bond was broken.

sources.section: 4. The rise of Volgan and the fall of the capital

paragraphs.text: In the second millennium of the First Age Volgan invaded Mirolon and made it the opening of a vast conquest. With Aenor weakened and scattered, his victories were swift and terrible. He gathered his forces in the Ember Lands, made alliances with rulers of the eastern and southern lands, and opened dealings with powers of the Dark Lands. Not every Easterling, southerner, Dark Lands people or monster joined him.

sources.section: 4. The rise of Volgan and the fall of the capital

paragraphs.text: His armies held corrupted elves, orcs, goblins, eastern and southern men, demons, devils of realms unknown to men, dragons and many Great Spirits. He also released the Damned Spirits from deep beneath the mountains and the world below, and they brought dangers that most men had never met.

sources.section: 4. The rise of Volgan and the fall of the capital

paragraphs.text: Volgan used his stronghold in the Ember Lands and the fleets of his allies to cross the waters that had turned back earlier explorers. Eastern client rulers gave him ships, landing places, food and roads through the Dark Lands. He struck at distant Aenoran holdings to keep the defenders scattered before he drove at the crownlands, and his captains seized food stores and ports wherever they could.

sources.section: 4. The rise of Volgan and the fall of the capital

paragraphs.text: Aenor’s defences failed. The reigning king died, and Volgan’s armies took the capital, and the kingdom stood on the edge of collapse. With the royal city were lost its archives, its records of succession, its sacred objects and the authority that had held much of the kingdom together. The scholars do not agree whether the royal city of that age stood where Parim stands now.
paragraphs.note: The losses with the royal city (archives, records of succession, sacred objects, authority) are proposed; the king’s death, the fall of the capital and the near collapse are established.

sources.section: 4. The rise of Volgan and the fall of the capital

plate.subject: banners of men, elves, dwarves and giants in one camp

paragraphs.text: In the catastrophe a new king rose in Aenor: Edran, who is remembered as the greatest king of men after Aen. His defining work was the Grand Alliance against Volgan. He rallied men, elves, dwarves, giants, spirits and many other peoples from across Aoaz against the dark armies.

sources.section: 5. The new king and the Grand Alliance

paragraphs.text: The alliance drew its strength from the West Lands, the North Lands, the islands, the Magical Lands and even parts of the Dark Lands. Elves came from several regions. Lorien, the great king of the Gala elves of the Lands of the Sun, led a formidable army in person. Edran knew little of the Gala before they met; it was one of the first great meetings of their courts.

sources.section: 5. The new king and the Grand Alliance

paragraphs.text: Edran the Gatherer came of a branch of Aen’s line that no one had expected to inherit. His right was disputed, but a surviving council of nobles, soldiers and refugees crowned him outside the occupied capital. He had to win allies before he could hope to retake anything.

sources.section: King Edran, with proposed details of his early reign

paragraphs.text: His gift was to lead peoples who trusted neither Aenor nor one another. Under the Charter of Free Banners every member kept its own crown and banner and a seat in the alliance council, and all served under one wartime command that Edran held by agreement, not by right. The North Lands stayed allies, not subjects. The western realms held that fighting Volgan beside Aenor did not mean accepting Aenor’s old claims.

sources.section: King Edran, with proposed details of his early reign

paragraphs.text: Those concessions cost Edran the support of hard-line Aenoran nobles, and they made the Grand Alliance possible. The western commanders fought because an unchecked Volgan would be worse for their peoples, and they remembered his promises. The elves of the Magical Forest, who know no hereditary crown, came as free peoples. Lorien came as an ally, not as a servant of Aenor.

sources.section: King Edran, with proposed details of his early reign

paragraphs.text: The alliance broke Volgan at Dardan, where many died and allied spirits stripped his power and cast him into the Void. It then tried to conquer his Ember Lands, where Elzon’s defence cost it dearly. The elves had opposed that invasion, and its failure broke the unity of the alliance.

plate.subject: an immense battlefield turning to wasteland, no landmarks

paragraphs.text: Dardan was the decisive battle of the First Age war against Volgan. It claimed millions of lives and left a wasteland behind. The Grand Alliance defeated Volgan there, and other spirits stripped his power and banished him to the Void. No map of this age marks the field, and the scholars do not agree where it lay.

The scholars tell it as the Thirteen Days of Dardan. In the first three days the lines closed. Orc and goblin legions struck the forward positions, eastern and southern horsemen sought the open flanks, and corrupted elves broke the defensive spells, while Edran held the mixed centre. In the next three, dark dragons burned the supply stores, and dwarven engineers and giants of Hirolon held the crossings and built new ones under attack.

sources.section: Proposed course of the battle: the Thirteen Days of Dardan

paragraphs.text: Ships of the islands brought food, weapons and the wounded where the inland roads could not cope, and thousands died only to keep the alliance in its place. On the seventh day the earth opened: Volgan loosed the Damned Spirits from beneath the hills. Great Spirits held the breaches while the dwarves collapsed the tunnels, and some of those spirits remain sealed beneath the waste of Dardan still.

sources.section: Proposed course of the battle: the Thirteen Days of Dardan

paragraphs.text: On the tenth day, after the alliance had taken its worst losses, Lorien sent in the host of the Gala elves. They met the corrupted elves and held back the dragons, and the elves of the Magical Lands fought beside them, though their customs differed. A failing flank was restored, and Edran could strike back.

sources.section: Proposed course of the battle: the Thirteen Days of Dardan

paragraphs.text: Then allied Great Spirits began a rite beneath the field. Volgan had spent much of his strength holding his armies together and calling up the deep beings, and they turned that against him. On the last day Edran led the final attack to hold the way open, and Volgan’s guard was cut off from him. Several Great Spirits together stripped him of the strength he could use in Aoaz and cast him into the Void. He was not destroyed, and the spirits who did it paid a heavy price.

sources.section: Proposed course of the battle: the Thirteen Days of Dardan

paragraphs.text: Volgan’s army broke as one host; some fled, surrendered or fought to the end, and others held together under surviving captains. The cities and fields around Dardan were ruined. No god won that day: the Holy Seven, the Creator and Zol did not intervene, and the victory belonged to men, elves, dwarves, giants, island fleets, the free peoples of the West and the Dark Lands, and the allied spirits together.
paragraphs.note: The break of the army and the ruin of the land are established; the account of the captains and the statement that no god intervened come from the proposed account.

sources.section: Proposed course of the battle: the Thirteen Days of Dardan

plate.subject: an army retreating through heat-haze and ash

paragraphs.text: Volgan’s banishment was an immense victory, but the Ember Lands were neither destroyed nor conquered. King Edran wanted to enter and hold them, so that Volgan’s dominion could never threaten Aoaz again. The elven leaders opposed it. The alliance pressed on anyway.

sources.section: 7. The failed conquest of the Ember Lands

paragraphs.text: Elzon had gathered and prepared what was left of Volgan’s forces. The invasion met fierce resistance and was driven back with heavy losses. The land itself and the exhaustion of the alliance made further conquest too costly, and the attack was given up. Many elves died in that invasion, after all they had already given at Dardan, and the king’s decision badly damaged the trust between men and elves.

sources.section: 7. The failed conquest of the Ember Lands

paragraphs.text: Elzon had foreseen that Volgan might fall. He had readied strongholds and fallback positions on the approaches, and he drew his troops back to coasts, passes and fortresses that could be held. He burned the stores near the frontier and used the weather, the heat and the hard ground. The alliance marched into land it could neither feed nor hold, and the defenders, fewer than before, had only to hold their own ground.

Edran held the invasion necessary to prevent a return. Lorien judged it a mistake once the great threat was gone, and Sirael and other elven leaders warned that the troops could not endure another great struggle. When Elzon’s counterattack struck the overstretched host, their warnings were proved right. Lorien’s people paid for a decision they had opposed.

The war ended when the last members of the alliance abandoned the invasion and went home, and Year 1675 closed the First Age. The invasion is the central stain on Edran’s great reign. The records of Aenor praise the saviour of the crown; the chronicles of the Gala and the Magical Lands remember his needless pursuit; those of the West and the Dark Lands remember the price he promised for their loyalty.
paragraphs.note: The end of the war and the year are established; the three traditions of memory are proposed.

sources.section: 8. The end of the age and its legacy

paragraphs.text: That mistake destroyed the confidence another Grand Alliance would have needed. When Elzon invaded Aenor at the end of the Second Age, the elven kingdoms sent no armies to help men.

Afrit played a great part in Volgan’s defeat in the First Age, and no one knew it. In secret he gathered demons, spirits, men and elves against Volgan and set them on the dark lord’s path, and their part in the Grand Alliance’s victory went unrecognised.

He did not act from loyalty to Aenor, nor as a true ally of the alliance. He used the war to destroy a rival far stronger than himself, and to weaken both Volgan and the survivors, so that he could rise in the age that followed. He expected an exhausted kingdom to be easier to take later.

His hidden hand does not undo what the alliance won. The armies of men, elves, dwarves and giants, and the spirits who bound Volgan, still fought and died at Dardan. No chronicle tells how Afrit hid his alliances, or how much Edran, Lorien and the other commanders suspected.
